name: Graham's Law of Effusion
statement: Lighter gases escape through a tiny hole faster, at a rate set by one over the square root of their molar mass.
statementAccent: one over the square root of their molar mass
meaning: Graham's law states that the rate at which a gas effuses, or escapes through a tiny opening, is inversely proportional to the square root of its molar mass, or equivalently its density. Lighter molecules effuse faster: a gas four times heavier effuses at half the rate. The same relation applies approximately to diffusion, the spreading and mixing of gases. Discovered by Thomas Graham in the nineteenth century and explained by the kinetic theory of gases, the law is simple but consequential, most dramatically as the basis for separating the isotopes of uranium in the making of the first atomic bombs.
mechanism: The law follows directly from kinetic theory. At a given temperature all gases have the same average kinetic energy, so setting the kinetic energies of two species equal shows that a molecule's typical speed is inversely proportional to the square root of its mass: lighter molecules move faster. Since the rate of effusion is proportional to how fast molecules travel, it too scales as one over the square root of the molar mass. For two gases at the same temperature and pressure, the ratio of their effusion rates equals the square root of the inverse ratio of their molar masses, or of their densities.

examples.text: Separating fissile uranium-235 from uranium-238 as gaseous uranium hexafluoride relies on Graham's law; the tiny mass difference gives a per-stage separation factor of about 1.0043, requiring thousands of stages, as at the Manhattan Project's K-25 plant.
Helium, far lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen of air, effuses through a small leak much faster, which is why helium balloons deflate more quickly than air-filled ones.
A gas four times heavier than another effuses at half the rate, since the rate goes as one over the square root of the molar mass.

variants.name: Effusion versus diffusion
variants.text: The law is exact for effusion, escape through an orifice small compared with the mean free path, and only approximate for diffusion, the collision-laden spreading of one gas through another.

variants.name: The density form
variants.text: Because density is proportional to molar mass at fixed temperature and pressure, the law can equally be written in terms of the square root of the ratio of densities.

whyItMatters: Graham's law is a simple, quantitative consequence of the kinetic theory of gases that connects a molecule's mass to how fast it escapes or spreads, and it carries outsized historical weight as the principle behind gaseous-diffusion isotope separation. That method, exploiting the minuscule mass difference between uranium isotopes as uranium hexafluoride, enriched the uranium for the first nuclear weapons and reactors. The law also illustrates a general lesson of kinetic theory, that at a given temperature lighter molecules simply move faster, with practical consequences from leaking balloons to industrial gas separation.

working.lead: Scale by inverse square root of mass
working.text: expect a gas's effusion rate to vary as one over the square root of its molar mass, so lighter gases escape faster.
take the ratio of two gases' effusion rates as the square root of the inverse ratio of their molar masses or densities.
use repeated effusion to enrich a lighter isotope, accepting that a tiny mass difference needs many stages.

limits: Graham's law is an idealisation, strictly valid for effusion through an orifice small compared with the mean free path and for ideal gases. It applies only approximately to diffusion, which involves many intermolecular collisions and concentration gradients and is more complex than simple effusion. It is fundamentally a statement about average molecular speeds, so it captures the mass dependence but not the detailed transport of interacting gases, and real gases deviate from ideal behaviour under conditions of high pressure or low temperature.
misreadings: Effusion, the escape of gas through a tiny orifice, is not the same as diffusion, the mixing and spreading of gases; the law is exact for the former and only approximate for the latter. The rate is inversely proportional to the square root of the molar mass, not to the molar mass itself, so a fourfold-heavier gas effuses at half, not a quarter, the rate. And the molar-mass and density forms are equivalent, since density is proportional to molar mass at the same temperature and pressure.
origin: Formulated by the Scottish chemist Thomas Graham, who established the effusion relation to molar mass in 1848, following his earlier work around 1831 relating effusion rate to gas density.
